description: Sol 48 is a three-member team, Devang, Samruddhi, and Archisa, participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 on November 14–15. We're interested in space science, NASA's open data, and building working projects together.
summary:
Imagine an astronaut on Mars with a few hours of air, a sunset they can't miss, and one question, how far can I go and still make it back? Sol-48 answers it before the first step.

It is a tool for planning and rehearsing walks on Mars. You start on a 3D globe with ground ice, minerals, caves, radiation and dust, and a site finder ranks 200 candidate sites.  Add stops,  get a planned route with the time, energy and radiation dose, the turn back point and the last place you can still get home from. Rehearse it turn by turn, in real rover panoramas and a helmet visor with SOS, all offline.
details:
What is Sol-48:
Imagine an astronaut stepping off the ladder on Mars. They have a few hours of air, a sunset they can't miss, and a list of rocks the science team wants. The question in their head is simple: how far can I go and still make it back? We built Sol-48 to answer that before anyone takes a step.

NASA has mapped Mars in incredible detail, but that knowledge is spread across dozens of missions and instruments, and most of it is measured in kilometres. A walk happens one metre at a time. Sol-48 brings it all into one place at the scale of footsteps and turns it into clear rules: don't climb to tough locations, watch your budget, turn back here, be home before dark. The crew gets to walk the route once before they walk it for real.

It starts with the whole planet. In Explore you spin a 3D Mars and turn on what you care about: ground ice in the top metre (SWIM), places where water once changed the rock into clays, sulfates and carbonates, olivine, geology, caves, radiation, dust storms over the years and surface temperature. The strongest signals are marked on the globe so they stand out. If you are still deciding where to go, the site finder ranks 200 candidate sites, and you choose how much terrain, climate, solar power, protection and science matter to you. Every site shows its HiRISE photo and the 100 km area a crew could explore around it, the same idea NASA used in its 2015 study of human landing sites.

You can zoom into a 4 by 4 km area mapped at 1 m: Gale crater at the foot of Mount Sharp, Jezero crater or McLaughlin crater. Place a Shelter (a habitat or a pressurised rover) and click where you want to stop. Sol-48 draws the route and tells you what it will cost. It never sends you up anything steeper than 20 degrees. It works out the time, the climb, the energy your body will burn (the Pandolf walking equation with Santee's 2003 downhill correction, at Mars gravity) and the radiation dose based on what Curiosity's RAD instrument has measured. Most importantly it marks the turn back point, the last place where you still have enough left to walk home. Every walk also has to end before sunset, which we calculate with NASA's Mars24 method.

After that you rehearse it. Walk replays the plan on 3D terrain with turn by turn directions, where the Sun is, and real rover photos at the stops. You can also step inside NASA's 360 degree rover panoramas and move between them. Visor shows what the astronaut would see in their helmet: heading, next stop, time left, a warning that builds up from "on pace" to "return to shelter", an SOS button, and when the next orbiter passes overhead to relay a message. Those passes come from NASA's own spacecraft orbit data.

All of this runs on data we prepared ourselves. A Python pipeline turns raw NASA products into map tiles, and the app is a static site, so it also works offline. That matters, because there is no internet on Mars.

We also tried something ambitious and we want to be honest about how it went. We trained a model to predict walkable ground using the path Curiosity actually drove at Gale, around 49,000 positions, and tested it on Perseverance's path at Jezero, which it had never seen. It did a little better than slope alone (0.551 against 0.504), but not by the margin we had set for ourselves. So we did not let it plan routes. A simple rule based on slope and roughness does that, one a crew can understand and check, and the model stays in the app as an experimental layer

How we built it:

The app is written in TypeScript with React, Vite and CesiumJS, using Cesium Mars for the 3D terrain and PMTiles for our own map layers. The pipeline is in Python with rasterio, numpy, scipy, spiceypy, scikit learn, LightGBM, Pillow and boto3. It is hosted on Vercel with the data on Cloudflare R2, and we tested it with Vitest, pytest and Playwright screenshots. The data comes from HiRISE, CTX, CRISM, THEMIS, TES, MOLA, HRSC, MCS, RAD, REMS, MEDA, SWIM, MOCAAS, the USGS geology map, the MGC3 cave catalogue, NAIF SPICE, and Curiosity and Perseverance.

We worked across three laptops, two Windows and one Mac, connected with Tailscale. AI agents did a lot of the building: Claude, Codex and Gemini, coordinated through Orca ADE. One agent broke the work into tasks and handed each one to another agent working in its own copy of the code. We reviewed every result, read the tests, checked the screenshots and approved every change ourselves.

What's creative about it:

We treat a Marswalk as a budget, not just a map. Every step costs something, and you can see exactly where the safe limit is.

One plan goes all the way through: from the planet, to a site, to a single stop, to the view inside a helmet.

We put real rover history to work. Curiosity's and Perseverance's paths became our test, and their panoramas let you stand where they stood.

We report our own failure. When our model didn't clear our bar, we said so and kept the rule a crew can trust.

What we kept in mind:

Safety first: hard limits a crew can check, a clear turn back point and no walking in the dark.

Honesty: our budgets are planning estimates, the visor is a simulation, the colour on greyscale images is labelled as a tint and not true colour, a rover's path is only a stand in for a person's, and 1 m data can't see rocks smaller than about a metre.

No internet on Mars, so everything works offline.

The right scale for the job: every layer is shown at its real resolution.

Open data, properly credited, including HRSC, SWIM and MOCAAS.

Easy to use: day and night themes, a short guided tour you can skip, and layouts that work on a laptop or a tablet.

The impact we hope for:

We would love mission planners to use something like this to choose where to land and where crews should walk, and for crews to know before they leave exactly when to turn around. Science teams could weigh what a stop is worth against what it costs to reach it. And anyone, a student or just someone who loves Mars, can stand on real surface data and see the planet at human scale.
